entry.breathQuote: I started watching Attack on Titan thinking I knew who the monsters were. By the end, I was more interested in asking why people become what they become, and how easily I can call someone wrong when I only know half their story.

reflection.quote: What stayed with me wasn't the question of who was right. It was how quickly my idea of right and wrong changed when I was finally shown what the other side had lived through.
reflection.whatIKept: I learned to be more careful with certainty. When I first see someone doing something I think is wrong, my first instinct is usually to judge the action. AOT made me think about what came before it. What did they lose? What were they taught? What were they afraid of? That doesn't make every action acceptable. It just reminds me that understanding someone and agreeing with them are two completely different things.
reflection.definingScene: The ocean. I had spent so much time watching the characters fight just to reach that moment. So when they finally got there, I expected it to feel like freedom. Instead, Eren looked across the ocean and saw another enemy. That stayed with me because sometimes we imagine that one achievement, one place, or one answer will finally make everything feel complete. Then we reach it and realize the world is still there.
reflection.whoItMadeMeThinkAbout: People I have judged from a distance. People whose decisions I couldn't understand because I didn't know what they had been through. And eventually, myself — especially the moments when I felt completely certain that my way of seeing something was the only reasonable one.

thoughtCascade.thought: They're the monsters. We just need to survive.
If both sides think they're protecting themselves, who gets to decide who's the villain?

cinematicMoment.title: The Basement.
cinematicMoment.body: I thought the basement would finally explain everything. It did. But instead of making the story simpler, it made it much bigger. The truth didn't feel like an answer. It felt like a responsibility. Once I knew what was outside the walls, I couldn't go back to believing the world was as simple as I had imagined it.

memoryCards.question: What stayed with me after the screen went dark?

cards.title: The Ocean
cards.text: I thought reaching the ocean meant reaching freedom. Then I realized that sometimes we reach the thing we wanted and discover that our real struggle has only changed.

cards.title: The Other Side
cards.text: The people I hated stopped being ideas. They became people with names, families, fear, childhoods and reasons. Understanding them didn't make their actions right. It made judging them harder.

cards.title: The Walls
cards.text: The walls weren't only around the characters. I started noticing the walls I build in my own head whenever I decide I already know the truth.

altMemories.question: What quietly changed?
altMemories.heading: I became suspicious of certainty.
altMemories.body: I used to think being sure meant I understood something. AOT made me realize that sometimes certainty just means I haven't looked from far enough away. Now, when I feel completely justified, I try to ask what I might be missing.
altMemories.caption: Being certain and being right are not the same thing.

altMemories.question: What did freedom become?
altMemories.heading: Something heavier than I expected.
altMemories.body: I used to think freedom mostly meant being able to choose whatever I wanted. AOT made me think about what comes after the choice. If my freedom hurts someone else, I still have to carry that consequence. Having a choice doesn't remove responsibility.
altMemories.caption: Freedom also means owning what you choose.

pullQuote.text: I don't need to agree with someone to understand them. And understanding them doesn't mean I have to excuse what they did.

firstImpression.heading: I thought I knew the story
firstImpression.body: Titans. Walls. Survival. Revenge. I thought I was watching a story about humans fighting monsters. I had already decided who deserved to win.

whatShifted.heading: Then the world got bigger
whatShifted.body: The further I went, the harder it became to divide everyone into good people and bad people. The enemy had a history. They had families. They were scared too. They had their own version of the story.

whatStayed.heading: I stopped trusting simple answers
whatStayed.body: AOT didn't make me believe that everyone is secretly good. It made me more careful about deciding that someone is simply bad. There can be reasons behind a person without those reasons becoming an excuse.

items.line: when I start turning someone into a villain before I actually understand what happened.
whether I know enough to be as certain as I feel.
to understand the reason behind someone's decision before deciding what that person is.
that understanding someone does not require me to agree with them.

characters.name: Eren Yeager
characters.mirror: I understood his desire for freedom more than I expected to. That's what made his journey uncomfortable. He reminded me that wanting something deeply doesn't automatically make everything I do for it right.

characters.name: Erwin Smith
characters.mirror: Erwin made me think about decisions where there is no clean answer. Sometimes leadership means choosing between terrible options and accepting that someone will have to carry the weight of that choice.

characters.name: Levi Ackerman
characters.mirror: Levi showed me a kind of strength that doesn't need to be loud. Do what needs to be done. Protect who you can. Accept what you couldn't save. Keep moving without pretending it didn't hurt.

notes.text: Maybe the scariest wall is the one I stop noticing.
notes.footer: What the walls meant to me

notes.text: AOT didn't make me believe everyone is good. It made me more careful about deciding who isn't.
Sometimes the truth doesn't make life easier. It just makes ignorance impossible.
Freedom sounds beautiful until you realize someone has to live with the consequences of what you choose.

ideas.application: I try to remember that two people can make completely different decisions because they are looking at completely different worlds. Before judging someone's decision, I want to understand the information, fear and experiences behind it.
When I feel completely certain that I understand someone or something, I try to look again. Not because every side is equally right, but because my view is still only one part of the picture.

Having the freedom to choose doesn't mean the choice is free. Every choice affects something outside of me, and growing up means learning to carry those consequences instead of only celebrating the freedom.
I learned that understanding why someone became who they are doesn't mean I have to defend what they did. I can understand the person, reject the action, and still refuse to reduce them to one label.

continueJourney.because: Because AOT left me with a strange kind of doubt. Not doubt in everything, but doubt in the part of me that thinks it has already understood everything. It made me want stories that keep asking what happens when the answer isn't as simple as I wanted it to be.

recommendations.title: Vinland Saga
recommendations.reason: What happens when you stop measuring strength by how many enemies you can defeat.

recommendations.title: Code Geass
recommendations.reason: What happens when you knowingly become the person the world will hate because you believe the future you want is worth the cost.
